S1.concept: Copilot predicts the next likely words from patterns and the context you give it. It does not look things up or know your work. You direct it and check it.

spark.hook: A messy mock exception log becomes a clean summary. Is it understanding, or predicting from what we pasted?

segments.label: Segment 1
segments.focus: What a model, tokens and context are, shown through the exception log demo

segments.label: Segment 2
segments.focus: First guided prompts on mock material from each learner's function; spotting limits

S1.build: Each learner runs three guided prompts on a mock document from their own function and notes where the output helped or slipped.
howTo: Open Copilot Chat and paste a short mock or anonymised document.
Ask for a five-bullet summary for a named reader.
Remove half the text and ask again; compare the answers.
Mark anything the output states that the source does not contain.
reflect: What surprised you about how Copilot produces an answer?
Where did the output sound confident but go beyond the source?
Which word now describes AI better for you: magic, threat, or predictor?

S2.concept: The output is only as good as the instruction. Role, context, audience and format turn a generic answer into one you can use.

spark.hook: Two prompts for the same job description: one vague, one precise. Spot the difference before we reveal it.

segments.label: Segment 1
segments.focus: Vague versus precise asks; adding role, context, audience and format one at a time

segments.label: Segment 2
segments.focus: Live comparison exercises on a task from each learner's own function

S2.build: Learners write a vague and a precise prompt for one task in their function, run both, and record what changed.
howTo: Write the task as you would say it aloud in one line.
Add who Copilot should act as and who will read it.
Add the context, the constraints and the format you want back.
Run both versions and note three differences side by side.
reflect: Which single addition to your prompt changed the output most?
When output disappoints, do you now blame the tool or the instruction?
What will you add to every prompt from tomorrow?

S3.concept: Safe use is part of the skill. Know which data is permitted, where output fails, and how to verify it before anyone relies on it.

spark.hook: A risk register summary reads perfectly. One control owner and one rating are wrong. Can you find them?

segments.label: Segment 1
segments.focus: Permitted work data, external tool boundaries, UK GDPR and Consumer Duty in practice

segments.label: Segment 2
segments.focus: Verification techniques, the readiness diagnostic and personal do and do-not lists

S3.build: Learners sort sample work items from their function into permitted, anonymise-first and never, then draft their personal do and do-not list.
howTo: Before pasting, ask: is this customer-identifiable, confidential or unapproved?
Replace names, account numbers and addresses with neutral placeholders.
Ask Copilot to quote the source line behind each key claim.
Check every figure, name and date against the original yourself.
reflect: Complete the mindset pulse: where do you stand on checking AI output?
Which item on your do-not list would you most likely have missed?
Who is accountable when AI output is wrong: the tool or you?

SELF.concept: Consolidate the foundation at your own pace: how generative AI works, why instructions matter, and why governance shapes every use.

segments.label: Self-paced
segments.focus: Curated reading and short videos on generative AI fundamentals, completed before Session 4

howTo: Work through the curated reading and videos in the order given.
Note one idea that confirms and one that challenges your view.
Write three questions about using AI in your own role.
Bring your consolidated notes to Session 4.
reflect: What do you now understand about AI that you did not three sessions ago?
Which fear or assumption about AI has shifted, and why?

S4.concept: Copilot becomes useful when you bring it real, permitted tasks from your own role, try it, and judge the result honestly.

spark.hook: Mock case notes become a structured credit memo draft. The underwriter still decides.

segments.label: Segment 1
segments.focus: Trainer demonstration on document and email tasks drawn from learners' roles

segments.label: Segment 2
segments.focus: Learner practice on three permitted tasks; trainer observes and corrects

S4.build: Each learner picks three recurring document or email tasks from their role and builds a working prompt for each on permitted material.
howTo: List three tasks you repeat weekly that involve drafting or summarising.
Prepare a permitted or mock version of the input for each.
Run a first prompt, then refine it at least twice.
Save the version that needed the least editing.
reflect: How many attempts did your best prompt take, and what changed each time?
Which task surprised you by working well, or by not working?
What would you try differently if you started again?

S5.concept: Notes, summaries and follow-ups can be drafted from pasted or exported meeting notes. Copilot here does not join or record meetings.

spark.hook: Rough notes from a product meeting become a summary, action list and follow-up draft. Pasted, not recorded.

segments.label: Segment 1
segments.focus: From pasted notes to summary, decisions and actions; what Copilot Chat can and cannot see

segments.label: Segment 2
segments.focus: Drafting follow-ups and responses that hold up without heavy editing

S5.build: Learners take mock or anonymised meeting notes from their function and build a tested summary-and-follow-up workflow.
howTo: Paste or upload your own typed or exported meeting notes.
Ask for decisions, actions with owners, and open questions separately.
Ask for a follow-up message in your team's usual tone.
Check every action and owner against your notes before sending.
reflect: How much editing did the follow-up need, and why?
What did you add to your prompt to reduce that editing?
Where would you not trust a summary without rereading the notes?

S6.concept: Structured prompts give predictable results. Role, context, constraints and an explicit output format are patterns you can repeat on purpose.

spark.hook: Same mock variance table, two prompts. One returns prose; the other returns board-ready commentary in a fixed format.

segments.label: Segment 1
segments.focus: The four building blocks: role, context, constraints, output format

segments.label: Segment 2
segments.focus: Building and testing structured patterns on learners' own tasks

S6.build: Learners rebuild one of their S4 prompts into a structured pattern and test whether it gives consistent output across two inputs.
howTo: Label four sections: Role, Context, Constraints, Output format.
State the format exactly: table columns, bullet count or word limit.
Add what to leave out, such as speculation or unstated figures.
Run the same pattern on two different inputs and compare.
reflect: Did structure make the output more consistent across inputs?
Which constraint saved you the most editing?
Which pattern would you reuse tomorrow without changing it?

S7.concept: A prompt that works once is personal; a template with clear placeholders and instructions is something the whole team can reuse.

spark.hook: One analyst's QC summary prompt becomes a template anyone in the team can fill in and trust.

segments.label: Segment 1
segments.focus: What makes a prompt reusable: placeholders, instructions, examples and limits

segments.label: Segment 2
segments.focus: Turning working prompts into a personal template set and testing it with a peer

S7.build: Learners convert their best working prompts into templates with placeholders and usage notes, then a peer tests one cold.
howTo: Replace task-specific details with bracketed placeholders, such as [period].
Add a one-line note on when to use and not use it.
Include the required checks the user must do on the output.
Ask a peer to run it without help and note confusion.
reflect: What did your peer misunderstand in your template?
Which of your prompts is ready for someone else to use?
How does writing for others change how you write prompts?

S8.concept: Copilot can extract, compare and summarise across long or messy documents, provided you set the questions and check against the source.

spark.hook: Three long mock vendor responses, one requirement list. A comparison table appears; which cells would you check?

segments.label: Segment 1
segments.focus: Extraction and comparison techniques; working within upload and length limits

segments.label: Segment 2
segments.focus: Building two research workflows on long permitted documents from learners' functions

S8.build: Learners build two research workflows, one extraction and one comparison, on long permitted or mock documents from their function.
howTo: Upload the documents, or paste long text in labelled sections.
Give a fixed list of questions or criteria to extract against.
Ask for a table with a source reference per cell.
Spot-check at least three cells against the original document.
reflect: Where did the extraction miss or merge information?
How did giving fixed criteria change the quality of the comparison?
Which long-document task will you test again this week?

S9.concept: Notes and data become useful when turned into structured output: tables, comparisons and action lists someone can act on.

spark.hook: Two hundred mock survey comments become a theme table with examples and suggested actions.

segments.label: Segment 1
segments.focus: From unstructured notes and data to tables, comparisons and action lists

segments.label: Segment 2
segments.focus: Building and testing one reporting workflow in each learner's function

S9.build: Learners build one reporting workflow that turns their function's notes or data into a structured table and action list.
howTo: Paste anonymised notes or data with a short description of each column.
Specify the table structure and the order of rows.
Ask for actions only where the data supports them.
Recount at least one figure or theme by hand.
reflect: Did the structure reveal anything the raw notes hid?
Which part of the report still needs your judgement?
How would you improve the prompt for next month's run?

S10.concept: Redesigning a task means mapping every step first, then deciding which steps AI drafts, which a human does, and where checks sit.

spark.hook: A month-end reconciliation note, mapped step by step. Where does AI help, and where must it not?

segments.label: Segment 1
segments.focus: Mapping a full task: inputs, steps, handoffs, checks and outputs

segments.label: Segment 2
segments.focus: Designing the AI-assisted version with human review points marked

S10.build: Learners map one full task from their role and design its AI-assisted version, marking AI steps, human steps and checkpoints.
howTo: List every step of the task today, including handoffs and checks.
Mark each step: AI drafts, human does, or human checks.
Write the prompt or template for each AI step.
Confirm every AI output passes a named human check.
reflect: Which step did you assume AI could do but decided it should not?
Where did mapping reveal waste you had not noticed?
How many separate prompts did one task really need?

S11.concept: A redesign is only real once it runs end to end on realistic input and you can show the before and after.

spark.hook: A first-cut audit programme built end to end from a mock process note, then checked by the auditor.

segments.label: Segment 1
segments.focus: Running the redesigned task end to end with the trainer

segments.label: Segment 2
segments.focus: Fixing weak steps and documenting the before and after

S11.build: Learners run their S10 redesign end to end on permitted or mock input, fix weak steps, and document the before and after.
howTo: Run each AI step in order, passing outputs forward by paste.
Note where you had to edit heavily or start again.
Rework the weakest prompt and rerun that step.
Record time and edits for the old and new versions.
reflect: Which step broke first, and what did you change?
Is the redesigned version genuinely better, or only different?
What would a colleague need to run this without you?

S12.concept: Prompts improve fastest under another person's eyes. Reviewing and being reviewed builds the judgement to iterate deliberately.

spark.hook: A feedback-summary prompt, reviewed by a peer, rewritten, rerun. Compare the two outputs side by side.

segments.label: Segment 1
segments.focus: A simple review checklist; breakout practice reviewing each other's prompts

segments.label: Segment 2
segments.focus: Improving prompts after review and retesting on permitted workplace examples

S12.build: In breakouts, learners exchange two prompts, review them against the checklist, then improve and retest their own on permitted examples.
howTo: Swap one prompt and its sample input with a partner.
Check role, context, constraints, format and data safety.
Suggest one change that would most improve the output.
Apply the feedback, rerun, and compare both outputs.
reflect: What did your reviewer see that you could not?
Which feedback point will you apply to all your prompts?
How comfortable are you now critiquing someone else's prompt?

S13.concept: AI output fails in predictable ways: invented detail, dropped items, wrong figures, overconfidence. Catching them, or not using AI, is the skill.

spark.hook: A shift handover summary drops one exception and invents a figure. How quickly can the room find both?

segments.label: Segment 1
segments.focus: Common failure modes, how to spot them, and tasks unsuited to AI

segments.label: Segment 2
segments.focus: Building and testing a personal verification checklist on learners' own outputs

S13.build: Learners audit three of their own earlier outputs for failure modes and turn what they find into a personal verification checklist.
howTo: Count items in the source and the output; confirm they match.
Trace every figure, name and date back to the source.
Ask Copilot what it was unsure about, then check those points.
Decide when the task is unsuitable for AI and note why.
reflect: Which failure mode did you find most often in your own outputs?
Name one task in your role where you would not use AI.
How has your habit of checking output changed since Stage 1?

CLINIC.concept: Clear what is blocking your practice before the applied stage, with the trainer and peers working through real problems.

segments.label: Single block
segments.focus: Learners bring blockers from their own practice and work them through with the trainer

CLINIC.build: Each learner brings one blocker, such as a prompt that will not hold or a data question, and works it through live.
howTo: State your blocker in one sentence with an example.
Show the prompt, the input type and the output you got.
Try the trainer's suggested fix live and compare.
Note any governance question to raise with the right OSBI contact.
reflect: Complete the mindset pulse: how has your use of AI changed so far?
Is your blocker cleared, and what will you try next?
Which workflow in your team are you ready to redesign?

S14.concept: Look at your workflows, not single prompts. Find at least three places where AI could change how work runs, and size each.

spark.hook: An onboarding checklist that takes hours to tailor per role. Is this a use case, and what is it worth?

segments.label: Segment 1
segments.focus: Spotting candidate use cases: repeated, text-heavy, reviewable, permitted data

segments.label: Segment 2
segments.focus: Sizing value: frequency, effort, quality and risk for each candidate

S14.build: Learners list at least three candidate use cases from their own workflow and size each by frequency, effort, quality and risk.
howTo: List tasks you repeat that involve drafting, summarising or comparing.
Filter out any needing customer-identifiable data or AI decisions.
For each, estimate frequency and current effort per occurrence.
Ask Copilot to challenge your sizing, then decide yourself.
reflect: Which candidate would change how your team works, not just you?
Which did you drop, and what boundary ruled it out?
Are you thinking about tasks or about workflows now?

S15.concept: A use case earns its place when your reporting manager agrees it matters. Prepare the case, have the conversation, choose one.

spark.hook: A one-page brief that turns an MIS summary idea into a five-minute manager conversation.

segments.label: Segment 1
segments.focus: Preparing the manager brief: problem, value, risk and ask

segments.label: Segment 2
segments.focus: Rehearsing the conversation, then selecting one use case for validation

S15.build: Learners draft a one-page brief on their three candidates, rehearse the manager conversation in pairs, and select one use case.
howTo: Paste your three sized candidates into Copilot Chat.
Ask for a one-page brief: problem, value, risk, ask.
Ask for three questions your manager is likely to raise.
Rewrite the brief in your own words before the meeting.
reflect: What did your manager value that you had underplayed?
Why is your selected use case worth redesigning the workflow for?
What evidence will you need to prove it worked?

S16.concept: A designed workflow has clear steps, inputs, prompts, human checks and an owner, so it runs the same way every time.

spark.hook: A product terms change triggers an FAQ refresh. Watch it designed as a repeatable, checked workflow.

segments.label: Segment 1
segments.focus: Workflow anatomy: trigger, inputs, AI steps, human checks, outputs, owner

segments.label: Segment 2
segments.focus: Designing each learner's selected use case as a step-by-step workflow

S16.build: Learners design their selected use case as a step-by-step workflow with inputs, prompts, human checks and an owner for each step.
howTo: Name the trigger that starts the workflow and the final output.
Write each step as input, action, output and owner.
Attach a prompt or template to every AI step.
Place a named human check before anything leaves the team.
reflect: How does the designed workflow differ from how the task runs today?
Which human check is most important, and who owns it?
Could a colleague run this workflow from your design alone?

S17.concept: Build the designed workflow and test it against real, permitted work. Design survives contact with live tasks only after iteration.

spark.hook: A vendor comparison workflow, tested on approved live responses. What broke on real documents that worked on mock ones?

segments.label: Segment 1
segments.focus: Building the workflow's prompts and templates with mentor input

segments.label: Segment 2
segments.focus: Testing against permitted live work and recording what needed fixing

S17.build: Learners build their workflow's prompts and templates, test them on permitted live work with mentor input, and log every fix.
howTo: Build each step's prompt from your S16 design.
Test on permitted live input, or approved anonymised versions.
Log each failure, its cause and the fix you made.
Rerun the full workflow once all fixes are in.
reflect: What did live work expose that mock data did not?
Is the workflow now reliable enough for daily use?
Which fix would matter most to a colleague adopting it?

S18.concept: You cannot prove an improvement without knowing the starting point. Measure how the task runs today, honestly, before changing it.

spark.hook: How long does a journal narrative really take today? Timing it honestly is the first step of proof.

segments.label: Segment 1
segments.focus: Choosing baseline measures: time, edits, errors, rework, turnaround

segments.label: Segment 2
segments.focus: Setting up and documenting each learner's baseline method and first readings

S18.build: Learners choose two or three baseline measures for their task and document how it runs today, with first readings.
howTo: Pick measures you can collect reliably: minutes, edits, errors, rework.
Time the current task on several real occurrences, not one.
Record conditions: input size, complexity, interruptions.
Write the baseline in a simple table your manager can read.
reflect: Did the real baseline differ from what you assumed?
Which measure will matter most to your manager?
How confident are you that the baseline is fair?

S19.concept: Compare after with before on the same measures. Estimate time, cost, quality or decision impact, and state the limits honestly.

spark.hook: Quality report summaries, before and after: minutes, rework and reviewer edits on the same measures.

segments.label: Segment 1
segments.focus: Measuring the redesigned task on the baseline measures

segments.label: Segment 2
segments.focus: Building the before-and-after comparison and stating its limits

S19.build: Learners measure their redesigned workflow on the S18 measures and build a before-and-after comparison with their own numbers.
howTo: Run the new workflow on comparable occurrences to the baseline.
Include review and correction time in the after figures.
Put before and after side by side for each measure.
Note sample size and anything that limits the comparison.
reflect: Does the evidence support the improvement you expected?
Which result would you be cautious about claiming, and why?
Has measuring changed how you think about the workflow?

S20.concept: A workflow that only you use is a personal habit. A one-page adoption plan turns it into something peers and teams can pick up.

spark.hook: A tested workflow becomes a one-page quick guide a peer can follow on day one.

segments.label: Segment 1
segments.focus: Who adopts first, what they need, and what gets in the way

segments.label: Segment 2
segments.focus: Writing and peer-testing the one-page adoption plan

S20.build: Learners write a one-page adoption plan for spreading their workflow to peers, including a quick guide and support steps.
howTo: Name the first peers or teams who could use the workflow.
List what they need: template, guide, example, checks.
Ask Copilot to draft a quick guide from your workflow design.
Test the guide with one peer and revise it.
reflect: Who in your team will adopt this first, and why them?
What barrier to adoption are you most worried about?
What would make a colleague choose to keep using it?

S21.concept: Every workflow carries risk. Name the responsible AI or data privacy risk in yours and define a practical mitigation someone will follow.

spark.hook: A control narrative for an AI-assisted workflow: the risk, the control, the owner, the evidence.

segments.label: Segment 1
segments.focus: Identifying responsible AI and data privacy risks in each learner's workflow

segments.label: Segment 2
segments.focus: Defining practical mitigations, owners and evidence

S21.build: Learners name the main responsible AI or data privacy risk in their workflow and write its mitigation, owner and evidence.
howTo: Walk your workflow step by step asking what could go wrong.
Pick the risk with the worst realistic consequence.
Write the control as a specific action with a named owner.
State what evidence shows the control is working.
reflect: Complete the mindset pulse: how has your view of AI risk changed?
Would your mitigation still work if a peer ran the workflow?
What risk would you warn every new adopter about?

INDEP.concept: Run your workflow on live, permitted work between sessions and capture the evidence that will make your case.

segments.label: Independent
segments.focus: Running the workflow on live work and producing progress artifacts across Stage 3

howTo: Run the workflow on permitted live tasks as they arise.
Log time, edits and issues each time you run it.
Save before-and-after examples, anonymised where needed.
Bring your log and artifacts to the next mentor session.
reflect: Is the workflow becoming your default way of doing the task?
What evidence from live use surprised you?

S22.concept: A workplace case brings evidence, the before and after, the adoption plan and the risk together into one argument others can act on.

spark.hook: Scattered findings become one insight report with a clear storyline. The same discipline builds your case.

segments.label: Segment 1
segments.focus: Case structure: problem, workflow, evidence, adoption plan, risk, ask

segments.label: Segment 2
segments.focus: Assembling each learner's complete workplace AI adoption case

S22.build: Learners assemble their stage outputs into one complete workplace AI adoption case with a clear storyline and evidence for each claim.
howTo: Gather your baseline, comparison, adoption plan and risk outputs.
Ask Copilot to propose a storyline outline from your materials.
Link every claim to a piece of your own evidence.
Rewrite the summary yourself so it sounds like you.
reflect: Could someone outside your team follow and act on your case?
Which claim is your strongest, and which needs more evidence?
How will this case help others adopt the workflow?

S23.concept: A strong case survives scrutiny. Mentor review finds the gaps; you close them and tighten every piece of evidence.

spark.hook: An auditor's eye on a case: every claim tested against its evidence. Apply it to your own.

segments.label: Segment 1
segments.focus: Mentor review of the full case against evidence and clarity criteria

segments.label: Segment 2
segments.focus: Closing gaps and tightening evidence for a reviewed, corrected case

S23.build: Learners act on mentor review: close evidence gaps, correct overstated claims, and produce a reviewed, corrected case.
howTo: List each claim in your case with its supporting evidence.
Ask Copilot to flag claims that lack clear support.
Decide yourself whether to add evidence or soften the claim.
Record every change made after mentor review.
reflect: Which gap would a sceptical reader have found first?
Is your case now honest about its limits?
What have you learnt about proving value, not just claiming it?

S24.concept: Practitioners can defend their case. Rehearse the five-minute presentation and prepare for the hard questions, if the panel is approved.

spark.hook: A loan policy change briefing, stress-tested by likely reviewer questions before it reaches committee.

segments.label: Segment 1
segments.focus: Shaping the five-minute presentation and anticipating panel questions

segments.label: Segment 2
segments.focus: Timed rehearsals with peer and mentor challenge, then final adjustments

S24.build: Learners rehearse their five-minute case, use Copilot to anticipate tough questions, and practise answers under peer challenge.
howTo: Cut your case to five minutes: problem, change, evidence, spread, risk.
Ask Copilot for the ten hardest questions a sceptical reviewer would ask.
Prepare short evidence-based answers in your own words.
Rehearse aloud with a timer and a peer challenging you.
reflect: Complete the mindset pulse: how have you changed since Session 1?
Which question would you least like to be asked, and why?
Who will you help adopt AI well in the next month?

useCases.title: Exception log to structured summary
useCases.scenario: A servicing team ends the day with a long, inconsistent exception log that the next shift must understand quickly.
useCases.input: A mock exception log with case references replaced by placeholders, pasted as text.
useCases.aiDoes: Groups exceptions by type, lists open items and suggested next steps in a short structured summary.
howTo: Paste the mock exception log into Copilot Chat.
Ask for exceptions grouped by type with counts.
Ask for open items and next steps as a table.
Compare counts in the summary with the original log.
useCases.humanCheck: The team member checks counts, categories and open items against the log before handover.
useCases.measure: Minutes to produce the handover summary; exceptions missed or miscounted.
useCases.boundary: Mock or anonymised logs only; no customer details pasted. AI summarises; people decide actions.

useCases.title: Vague versus precise job description prompt
useCases.scenario: HR needs a first draft job description for an operations analyst role and tries a one-line prompt first.
useCases.input: A mock role brief: responsibilities, required skills, team context and house style notes.
useCases.aiDoes: Produces two drafts, one from a vague prompt and one from a precise prompt, for side-by-side comparison.
howTo: Prompt once: write a job description for an operations analyst.
Prompt again with role, audience, mock brief and required format.
Compare both drafts for relevance, tone and missing content.
List which prompt elements caused each improvement.
useCases.humanCheck: HR checks accuracy, inclusive language and policy fit before any draft is used.
useCases.measure: Edits needed per draft to reach a usable job description.
useCases.boundary: Mock role brief only. AI drafts content; it does not screen, rank or select candidates.

useCases.title: Verifying a risk register summary
useCases.scenario: Risk needs a short summary of register movements for a committee pack, and the draft must be accurate.
useCases.input: A mock risk register extract with risks, ratings, owners and control status, uploaded as a file.
useCases.aiDoes: Summarises key movements and high-rated risks, citing the register row behind each statement.
howTo: Upload the mock register extract to Copilot Chat.
Ask for a summary of rating changes and high risks.
Ask it to cite the row behind each statement.
Check every rating and owner against the register.
useCases.humanCheck: The risk analyst verifies every rating, owner and movement against the register before use.
useCases.measure: Errors found per summary; minutes to verify the draft.
useCases.boundary: Mock or approved data only; no confidential register uploaded without approval. Ratings stay human judgements.

useCases.title: Structuring a credit memo draft
useCases.scenario: An underwriting support colleague turns scattered case notes into the standard credit memo structure before underwriter review.
useCases.input: Mock case notes and the blank credit memo section headings, pasted as text.
useCases.aiDoes: Arranges the notes under each memo heading, flags missing information and lists questions for the underwriter.
howTo: Paste the memo headings, then the mock case notes.
Ask it to place notes under headings without adding facts.
Ask for a list of missing information per section.
Check nothing was added beyond the notes.
useCases.humanCheck: The underwriter reviews the structured draft and makes every credit judgement and decision.
useCases.measure: Minutes to structure the memo draft; gaps flagged versus found later.
useCases.boundary: Mock notes only; no customer-identifiable data. AI structures text and never recommends or makes credit decisions.

useCases.title: Meeting notes to actions and follow-up
useCases.scenario: After a savings product meeting, a colleague must circulate decisions, actions and a follow-up message the same day.
useCases.input: Typed or exported mock meeting notes, pasted as text. Copilot Chat does not join or record meetings.
useCases.aiDoes: Drafts a summary of decisions, an action list with owners and dates, and a short follow-up message.
howTo: Paste your typed or exported meeting notes.
Ask for decisions, actions with owners, and open questions.
Ask for a follow-up message in a plain, professional tone.
Check each action and owner against your notes.
useCases.humanCheck: The note-taker confirms decisions, owners and dates with the notes before sending the follow-up.
useCases.measure: Minutes from meeting end to follow-up sent; edits made before sending.
useCases.boundary: Pasted or exported notes only; no Teams or Outlook integration. No customer data in notes.

useCases.title: Structured variance commentary
useCases.scenario: Finance writes monthly variance commentary on an MIS table and wants consistent format and tone each month.
useCases.input: A mock MIS variance table with actuals, budget and variances, pasted as text.
useCases.aiDoes: Drafts variance commentary in a fixed format: line item, variance, likely driver to confirm, and follow-up question.
howTo: Set the role: finance analyst writing for senior management.
Paste the mock variance table with column definitions.
Constrain it: only material variances, no invented drivers.
Specify the output as a four-column table.
useCases.humanCheck: The finance analyst confirms every figure and replaces suggested drivers with confirmed explanations.
useCases.measure: Minutes to first-draft commentary; edits needed to reach review standard.
useCases.boundary: Mock or approved figures only. AI drafts wording; drivers and figures are confirmed by finance.

useCases.title: Reusable QC summary template
useCases.scenario: Quality analysts each summarise sampling results differently; the team wants one template everyone can reuse.
useCases.input: Mock quality-check sampling results and a working prompt from one analyst.
useCases.aiDoes: Produces a consistent summary of sample size, pass rate, error themes and suggested SOP points to review.
howTo: Take the working prompt and mark the task-specific details.
Replace them with placeholders such as [sample period].
Add usage notes and the checks the user must do.
Have another analyst run it on different mock results.
useCases.humanCheck: The quality analyst checks rates and themes against sampling records before the summary is shared.
useCases.measure: Minutes per summary; variation in format between analysts.
useCases.boundary: Mock or anonymised sampling data only. AI summarises; quality judgements stay with analysts.

useCases.title: Comparing long vendor responses
useCases.scenario: Procurement must compare three lengthy RFP responses against a requirement list before a shortlist discussion.
useCases.input: Three mock vendor responses and a requirement list, uploaded as files.
useCases.aiDoes: Extracts each vendor's response per requirement into a comparison table with section references and gaps flagged.
howTo: Upload the requirement list and the three mock responses.
Ask for a table: requirement, vendor responses, source section.
Ask it to flag requirements a vendor did not address.
Spot-check several cells against the original responses.
useCases.humanCheck: The procurement lead verifies key cells against source documents; the evaluation panel makes the selection.
useCases.measure: Minutes to build the comparison table; cells found incorrect on spot-check.
useCases.boundary: Mock or approved documents only. AI extracts and compares; it does not score or select vendors.

useCases.title: Survey comments to theme report
useCases.scenario: Customer Insights receives hundreds of free-text survey comments and must report themes and actions to stakeholders.
useCases.input: Mock or anonymised survey comments with no customer identifiers, pasted or uploaded.
useCases.aiDoes: Groups comments into themes with approximate counts, example quotes and suggested actions in a table.
howTo: Paste or upload the anonymised comments.
Ask for themes with counts and two example comments each.
Ask for suggested actions only where comments support them.
Recount one theme by hand to check accuracy.
useCases.humanCheck: The insights analyst checks theme counts and quotes, and owns the conclusions shared.
useCases.measure: Minutes to produce the theme table; themes merged or missed on review.
useCases.boundary: Anonymised or mock comments only; strip names and account details before pasting.

useCases.title: Mapping the reconciliation note task
useCases.scenario: At month-end, accounts colleagues write reconciliation notes explaining breaks; the task is mapped before redesign.
useCases.input: A mock reconciliation summary with breaks and the current step-by-step process, pasted as text.
useCases.aiDoes: Helps list process steps and drafts a reconciliation note explaining each break from the supplied facts.
howTo: Paste your current process steps and ask for gaps.
Mark each step: AI drafts, human does, human checks.
Paste the mock break details and ask for a draft note.
Check each explanation against the reconciliation data.
useCases.humanCheck: The accountant confirms every break explanation and figure before the note is filed.
useCases.measure: Minutes per reconciliation note; steps removed or merged in the redesign.
useCases.boundary: Mock or approved figures only. AI drafts narrative; reconciliation and sign-off stay human.

useCases.title: First-cut audit programme, end to end
useCases.scenario: An auditor prepares a first-cut audit programme for a process review, using the redesigned AI-assisted steps.
useCases.input: A mock process description and a list of key risks, pasted or uploaded.
useCases.aiDoes: Drafts objectives, risks, test steps and evidence requests as a structured first-cut audit programme.
howTo: Paste the mock process description and key risks.
Ask for objectives and test steps linked to each risk.
Ask for evidence requests per test step.
Compare with your usual programme and note the differences.
useCases.humanCheck: The auditor reviews scope, tests and evidence requests; the audit lead approves the programme.
useCases.measure: Minutes to first-cut programme; test steps added or removed in review.
useCases.boundary: Mock or approved process material only. AI drafts; audit scope and conclusions are human.

useCases.title: Peer-reviewed feedback summary prompt
useCases.scenario: A learning colleague's prompt for summarising training feedback is reviewed and improved by a peer.
useCases.input: Mock session feedback forms, anonymised, and the colleague's original prompt.
useCases.aiDoes: Summarises feedback into strengths, improvement areas and suggested content changes, before and after the prompt is improved.
howTo: Run the original prompt on the mock feedback.
Peer reviews the prompt against the review checklist.
Apply the suggested change and rerun on the same feedback.
Compare the two summaries side by side.
useCases.humanCheck: The learning colleague checks the summary reflects the feedback before acting on it.
useCases.measure: Edits needed per summary, before and after peer review.
useCases.boundary: Anonymised or mock feedback only; no participant names pasted. AI summarises; people decide changes.

useCases.title: Catching errors in a handover summary
useCases.scenario: A shift handover summary looks complete, but one exception is missing and a figure does not match the log.
useCases.input: A mock exception log and its AI-generated handover summary containing planted errors.
useCases.aiDoes: Produces the handover summary; then, when asked, lists points where it was uncertain or inferred.
howTo: Count exceptions in the log and in the summary.
Trace each figure in the summary to the log.
Ask Copilot which statements were inferred, not stated.
Record each error type on your verification checklist.
useCases.humanCheck: The handing-over colleague reconciles the summary to the log before the next shift relies on it.
useCases.measure: Errors caught per summary; minutes spent verifying.
useCases.boundary: Mock logs only. Never pass on an AI summary without checking it against the source.

useCases.title: Sizing an onboarding checklist use case
useCases.scenario: HR tailors onboarding checklists by role by hand; is AI drafting worth pursuing, and how valuable is it?
useCases.input: A mock generic onboarding checklist and a short mock role profile.
useCases.aiDoes: Drafts a role-tailored onboarding checklist and helps list the factors for sizing the use case.
howTo: Paste the generic checklist and the mock role profile.
Ask for a tailored checklist with week-by-week steps.
Note how often this task occurs and its current effort.
Ask Copilot to challenge your sizing assumptions.
useCases.humanCheck: HR checks the checklist against policy and the hiring manager confirms role-specific steps.
useCases.measure: Checklists tailored per month; minutes per checklist today.
useCases.boundary: Mock profiles only; no new joiner personal data. AI drafts; HR owns onboarding decisions.

useCases.title: Manager brief for an MIS summary idea
useCases.scenario: A finance colleague wants manager backing to redesign how monthly MIS summaries are drafted.
useCases.input: The colleague's own notes on the problem, effort today and proposed change.
useCases.aiDoes: Drafts a one-page brief covering problem, value, risk and ask, plus likely manager questions.
howTo: Paste your notes on the problem and current effort.
Ask for a one-page brief: problem, value, risk, ask.
Ask for three questions your manager will likely raise.
Rewrite the brief in your own words.
useCases.humanCheck: The colleague checks every claim is accurate; the reporting manager validates the use case.
useCases.measure: Minutes to prepare the brief; manager questions anticipated versus asked.
useCases.boundary: No confidential figures needed in the brief. AI drafts; the manager validates and decides.

useCases.title: Designing an FAQ refresh workflow
useCases.scenario: When savings product terms change, the FAQs must be updated consistently, clearly and with compliance review.
useCases.input: Mock old and new product terms summaries and the current mock FAQ set.
useCases.aiDoes: Identifies FAQs affected by the change and drafts updated answers in plain English for review.
howTo: Paste the old terms, the new terms and current FAQs.
Ask which FAQs are affected by each change.
Ask for redrafted answers in plain, customer-friendly English.
Route drafts to the named reviewer before publishing.
useCases.humanCheck: The product owner checks accuracy; compliance reviews clarity and fairness under Consumer Duty before publishing.
useCases.measure: Minutes from terms change to FAQ drafts ready; FAQs missed.
useCases.boundary: Mock or approved product documents only. Nothing reaches customers without human and compliance review.

useCases.title: Testing a vendor comparison workflow
useCases.scenario: The vendor comparison workflow designed on mock data is now tested on approved, real RFP responses.
useCases.input: Approved RFP responses with confidential pricing removed, and the requirement list, uploaded.
useCases.aiDoes: Runs the comparison steps: extraction per requirement, gap flags and a neutral summary table.
howTo: Confirm the documents are approved for use in Copilot Chat.
Run each workflow step with your saved prompts.
Log where outputs failed on real documents.
Fix the prompt and rerun the failed step.
useCases.humanCheck: The procurement lead verifies extractions; the evaluation panel scores and selects vendors.
useCases.measure: Fixes needed per run; minutes per comparison.
useCases.boundary: Approved documents only; remove confidential terms if not permitted. AI never scores or selects vendors.

useCases.title: Baselining journal narrative effort
useCases.scenario: Before redesigning how journal narratives are written, accounts measures how long and how accurate they are today.
useCases.input: A simple timing log of current journal narratives written manually, plus sample mock narratives.
useCases.aiDoes: Helps structure the baseline table and summarises the timing log; it does not write the baseline.
howTo: Time several real journal narratives written the current way.
Record review comments and rework for each.
Paste the log and ask for a baseline summary table.
Check the table totals against your log.
useCases.humanCheck: The accountant confirms the baseline figures; the manager agrees the measures are fair.
useCases.measure: Minutes per journal narrative; review comments per narrative.
useCases.boundary: Timing logs contain no ledger or customer data. AI formats; measurements are recorded by people.

useCases.title: Before and after: quality report summaries
useCases.scenario: Quality compares time and rework on monthly quality report summaries before and after the AI-assisted workflow.
useCases.input: Baseline and post-change timing and rework logs, pasted as a simple table.
useCases.aiDoes: Builds a before-and-after comparison table and drafts a cautious narrative of the results and limits.
howTo: Paste the baseline and new measures in one table.
Ask for differences per measure, including review time.
Ask for a short narrative that states sample size and limits.
Recalculate the key differences yourself.
useCases.humanCheck: The quality analyst recalculates the comparison; the manager reviews claims before they are shared.
useCases.measure: Minutes per summary and rework items, before and after.
useCases.boundary: Only measurement data is pasted. No benefit is claimed beyond what the learner's own data shows.

useCases.title: Workflow to peer quick guide
useCases.scenario: A tested workflow needs a short guide so peers in other teams can adopt it without a training session.
useCases.input: The learner's own workflow design, prompts and checks, pasted as text.
useCases.aiDoes: Drafts a one-page quick guide: when to use, steps, prompts, required checks and where to get help.
howTo: Paste your workflow design, prompts and checks.
Ask for a one-page guide for a first-time user.
Test the guide with one peer who has not seen it.
Revise wherever the peer hesitated.
useCases.humanCheck: The workflow owner checks the guide is accurate and includes every required human check.
useCases.measure: Peers able to run the workflow from the guide alone.
useCases.boundary: Guide contains no work data. Prompts must keep the data rules and human review steps.

useCases.title: Control narrative for an AI workflow
useCases.scenario: Risk documents a responsible AI risk in an AI-assisted workflow as a control narrative, in register style.
useCases.input: The learner's workflow description and identified risk, with no confidential data.
useCases.aiDoes: Drafts a control narrative: risk description, cause, control, owner, frequency and evidence of operation.
howTo: Paste your workflow steps and the risk you identified.
Ask for a control narrative using register-style fields.
Make the control a specific action with a named owner.
Check the evidence would show the control is working.
useCases.humanCheck: The learner and risk colleague check the control is realistic, owned and evidenced.
useCases.measure: Control steps followed per workflow run; issues caught by the control.
useCases.boundary: Workflow descriptions only; no confidential data. AI drafts; risk owners decide ratings and controls.

useCases.title: Assembling an insight report storyline
useCases.scenario: Insights must turn scattered findings into one report with a clear storyline, mirroring how learners assemble their case.
useCases.input: Mock theme tables, key figures and notes from several insight analyses.
useCases.aiDoes: Proposes a report outline and storyline, linking each section to the supplied evidence.
howTo: Paste your findings, figures and notes in labelled sections.
Ask for a storyline outline: problem, evidence, insight, action.
Ask it to cite which input supports each section.
Rewrite the headline message yourself.
useCases.humanCheck: The insights analyst checks each claim is supported and owns the final conclusions.
useCases.measure: Minutes to a reviewable report draft; unsupported claims found in review.
useCases.boundary: Anonymised or mock findings only. AI structures the story; the analyst decides what is concluded.

useCases.title: Evidence-testing a findings summary
useCases.scenario: An auditor checks a draft findings summary to confirm every statement is backed by evidence before review.
useCases.input: A mock findings summary and a list of the evidence obtained, pasted as text.
useCases.aiDoes: Lists each claim, matches it to the supplied evidence and flags claims with weak or no support.
howTo: Paste the draft findings and the evidence list.
Ask for a claim-by-claim table with matching evidence.
Review each flagged claim and decide the fix yourself.
Record changes for the reviewer.
useCases.humanCheck: The auditor decides each fix; the audit lead reviews findings before they are issued.
useCases.measure: Unsupported claims found per summary; minutes to complete the check.
useCases.boundary: Mock or approved findings only. AI flags gaps; audit judgements and conclusions stay human.

useCases.title: Stress-testing a loan policy briefing
useCases.scenario: A lending colleague prepares to brief a policy change and must anticipate challenging questions from reviewers.
useCases.input: A mock summary comparing old and new loan policy wording.
useCases.aiDoes: Generates likely challenge questions by theme and drafts answer outlines that point back to the policy text.
howTo: Paste the mock policy comparison summary.
Ask for the ten hardest questions a sceptical reviewer would ask.
Ask for answer outlines citing the policy wording.
Rewrite the answers in your own words and rehearse.
useCases.humanCheck: The lending colleague checks answers against the policy; policy owners approve any interpretation.
useCases.measure: Questions anticipated versus questions actually asked.
useCases.boundary: Mock or approved policy text only. AI never interprets policy for credit decisions on cases.
